newsitem.title: USA: Albright concerned Israeli building hurts peace.
newsitem.headline: Albright concerned Israeli building hurts peace.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright expressed concern on Friday that new Israeli settlement construction was hurting efforts to restart Middle East peace negotiations.

"We are in the process of trying very hard to get the peace process back on track," she told reporters. "It is a very delicate moment in the whole situation where it's very important to do everything we can to rebuild the bonds of confidence and to get back to where we are dealing with a way to ultimately get a comprehensive peace."
"Within that context I expressed my concerns to (Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak) Mordechai about the thickening of the settlements," she said.

U.S. State Department officials said Mordechai told Albright during a meeting on Thursday that Israel was not actually building new Jewish settlements but only "thickening" existing settlements by constructing new buildings in them.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to meet with President Bill Clinton on Monday and offered earlier on Friday to meet in a Camp David-style summit with Arafat and Clinton if necessary to work out a peace deal.
"As soon as violence against us stops, we can clear up all outstanding questions in six months," Netanyahu said in an interview from Israel with Germany's ARD television.

"If we don't manage that within that time, then (Palestinian President Yasser) Arafat, President Clinton and I can try to settle the Israeli-Palestinian dispute in a sort of Camp David summit," he said.
A summit at the Camp David U.S. presidential retreat in 1978, overseen by then-President Jimmy Carter, led to Israel's peace treaty with Egypt, its first with an Arab state.

As Netanyahu made his proposal, Israeli troops in Hebron battled 400 Palestinian stone-throwers on a 16th consecutive day of Arab rage over a new Jewish settlement that Israel was building in disputed east Jerusalem.
U.S. officials said this week that reports of another possible summit now were premature.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said at a news briefing on Friday: "We have our own ideas for how to move this situation forward ... we're going to share those ideas first and foremost with the parties -- with Prime Minister Netanyahu and Chairman Arafat."

"We're very active," Burns said, "And as a result of the discussions with (Jordan's) King Hussein, Secretary Albright's telephone discussions with Prime Minister Netanyahu and Chairman Arafat, we are developing our own ideas and we're going to put them forward."
Mordechai said before completing his Washington visit on Friday that Arafat was not trying to halt violence in Israel.

"There is no doubt that if Arafat would decide and he would order these people and his security forces (to stop the violence), he will succeed ... and counter the terrorism activity," Mordechai told leaders of the B'Nai B'rith Jewish organisation.
But Mordechai said he had checked Israeli agencies shortly before his speech and "we haven't found any new initiative by Arafat ... to react against the terrorism."
